newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: Menem plays risky game by denying Argentine unrest.
newsitem.headline: Menem plays risky game by denying Argentine unrest.

text.p: Argentine President Carlos Menem's repeated denials that a general strike is another manifestation of festering unrest seems to be placing his party's fate at risk in 1997.

The Peronist leader, facing the greatest challenge to his free-market reforms since he came to power in 1989, brushed off the 36-hour strike and a rally in Buenos Aires' Plaza de Mayo on Thursday that attracted tens of thousands.

It followed a 24-hour walkout in August, an opposition-led "blackout" protest, a drubbing of Peronists in June voting for Buenos Aires mayor and surveys showing Menem's support below 20 percent, from 50 percent when he was reelected in May 1995.
Still, the 66-year-old president, convinced he must press ahead with new taxes and labour reforms despite 17.1 percent unemployment, refused to acknowledge a trend.

Menem, who angered unions and the opposition by dismissing the strike as an excuse for a long weekend, said he had flown over Buenos Aires by helicopter and, after peering down, could safely describe the protest as a "complete failure."

Asked in a newspaper interview published on Friday if he saw discontent among the people, he said, "No, no, no, maybe discontent in some leaders but not in the people. We'll wait until the next elections and see if the people are unhappy."
Argentines are expected to vote in October next year for 129 out of 257 representatives in the lower house of Congress in mid-term elections that could alter the balance of power.
The CGT, the largest trade federation, which organised the strike, has been traditionally pro-Peronist but is losing its will to back the Peronist administration.

"The government has to understand that this situation is now insufferable," CGT Secretary General Rodolfo Daer told the rally on Thursday. "You cannot govern with your back to the people because the people don't forgive betrayal."
The labour movement opposes tax hikes that Congress approved this week thanks to a governing party majority.

La Nacion newspaper's Atilio Cadorin wrote in a front-page column that the traditional relationship between the CGT and the government was no longer secure. "Once again the most important message is the one from the people," he said. "They have to be listened to."

Menem has faced five general strikes since coming to power -- three since his reelection last year. That rate, notes political analyst Rosendo Fraga, matches that of former President Raul Alfonsin of the Radical Party, who surrendered office to Menem several months early amid an economic crisis.

"These protests show social dissatisfaction is growing in Argentina," said Fraga, who heads a private think-tank. "It is a mistake to deny there are problems and he should recognise there are sectors of the population that are suffering."

The government, Fraga said, is hoping that the economy, now slowly on the mend after recession last year, will recover enough to create jobs before next year's polls. "Having a better economy will give them a better chance to win the election but not the certainty of winning."
